extracted.intended_audience: researchers and academic authors choosing journals for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers on how to evaluate journals to avoid predatory publishers and how to respond if they suspect a journal is predatory. Covers website signs, organizational memberships, contact and editorial verification, peer review standards, and post-submission actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website quality and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sloppiness is a hallmark of predatory journal websites: language that doesn't sound right, frequent spelling and grammar mistakes, and overall low professional standards. Also check how fees are presented on the website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for grammatical errors and questionable language as signs of a 'slapdash' effort. Verify that Article Processing Charges (APCs) are clearly stated and that fees are charged only after acceptance — a journal requesting an upfront submission fee may be predatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership verification in reputable organizations (DOAJ, COPE, OASPA, STM)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a journal claims membership in DOAJ, COPE, OASPA, or STM, you should verify that claim on the relevant organization's site or by contacting the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These organizations thoroughly screen applicants; confirming membership provides evidence of screening. Email the organizations to verify membership if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact information consistency and veracity
rubrics_metrics.description: A reputable journal will have contact information that checks out and matches the nation it claims to be headquartered in. Predatory journals often list contact info referencing a different country or unverifiable addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that listed phone country codes match the claimed country, Google-search the listed address, and observe response times to see if they align with the stated working hours/country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory journals may list established scholars without their permission or invent fake scholars with made-up credentials. Verify editorial board members' association with the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look up editorial board members' online profiles, LinkedIn pages, and institutional websites to see whether they mention the journal. If board members don't acknowledge affiliation, treat this as a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review process and publication schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: A credible journal runs a genuine peer review involving at least an editor and independent experts and allows appropriate time for evaluation. Predatory journals often have extremely quick timelines and superficial or no peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the journal’s peer review policy and publication schedule. Ask whether the stated process allows the necessary time for credible evaluation and whether independent expert review is described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Browse previous issues for scope and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory journals tend to publish articles on a wide range of unrelated topics and display poor editorial standards in past issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review past issues to see if articles fall far outside the stated scope (e.g., migraine therapy in a dermatology journal) and whether typos and errors are routinely overlooked — both indicate lack of quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive and indiscriminate solicitation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory journals often 'phish' for prospects through mass emails inviting submissions or editorial board membership, sometimes containing grammatical errors or unrealistic offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat unsolicited bulk invitations, especially those with poor language or overly flattering offers, as a warning sign. Aggressive solicitation is a characteristic of predatory behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and adherence to best editorial/publication practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory publishers prioritize self-interest over scholarship and are characterized by false/misleading information, deviation from best editorial and publication practices, and lack of transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the leading-scholar consensus definition (false/misleading info, deviation from best practices, lack of transparency, aggressive solicitation) as a high-level test when other checks are ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees: clarity, timing, and coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees should be transparent and charged only after an article has been accepted. Requesting upfront payment at submission or coercing payment (including withdrawal fees) are red flags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the timing and clarity of APCs on the website. If charged or demanded before acceptance, or if the journal demands a withdrawal fee or tries to coerce payment, decline to pay and treat the journal as suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of publishing in predatory journals (reputational risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing in predatory journals provides no meaningful scholarly value and can harm your career and institution’s reputation — hiring and promotion committees recognize predatory publications as strikes against candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider long-term reputational and professional consequences when choosing outlets; quantity of publications in suspect venues will not substitute for quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions to take if you suspect a submission is to a predatory journal
rubrics_metrics.description: If you realize after submission that the journal shows red flags (very fast 'peer review', immediate payment requests, not a COPE member), take steps to withdraw and avoid payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decline to pay fees and request withdrawal of your submission. If the publisher demands a withdrawal fee, resist paying and seek support from a supervisor. Contact COPE for guidance and assistance to pressure the journal if needed.
